# Ledger scale bench

Generated by `scripts/bench-ledger.ts` (`npx tsx scripts/bench-ledger.ts --sizes 10000` and `--sizes 100000`,
one size at a time, each in its own temp project under the container's own `/tmp`, deleted after) inside the
Node 22 clean-room container (`sidewise-test:node22`, `docker run --rm --memory 1500m -v $PWD:/app -w /app
sidewise-test:node22 ...`, host repo bind-mounted per the task's own instruction, container's own filesystem for
the generated ledgers) — **Node v22.23.3**, confirmed via the bench's own printed `node=` line, so `node:sqlite`
is real, not the fallback. Host machine: 24 vCPUs (x86_64), Linux 7.0.0-31-generic, a shared box (the same class
of machine the earlier 2026-09-26 research docs ran on, under similar load-sensitivity caveats — p50 is the
number this doc trusts, p95 is reported honestly but noisier). **Sizes are 10,000 and 100,000 runs only, both
real, both measured — 1,000,000 is a labelled extrapolation only (see below), never claimed as measured.**

Generator: `scripts/bench-ledger.ts`'s own `generateRealisticLedger` (self-contained — not
`test/gen/synthetic-ledger.ts`, whose `buildContractRun` hardcodes 1–3 keys/run for its own callers and isn't
reused here so that generator's behavior and timing stay untouched), 10–20 answer keys/run drawn from a bounded
pool so keys genuinely repeat, matching the realism gap `lab/research/2026-09-26-ledger-lookup-comparison.md`
found in the repo's default synthetic mix (index/log ratio ~0.03 there vs ~0.24 for real fake-provider `class`
runs).

## Bottom line

**The SQLite index is correct and self-healing at scale — every equivalence and self-heal test in
`test/unit/ledger-index.test.ts` and `test/unit/ledger-reuse-scale.test.ts` passes against the real engine, in
this same container — but on this run, on this shared machine, it does NOT cleanly clear the < 100 ms
per-call target at 100k the way the 2026-09-26 spike's own numbers did.** Point lookups that hit their fast path
(`reuseHit`, `findRunById`) land right at or just past 100 ms at 100k (93–130 ms p50); a genuine reuse **miss**
(no holder for the key — the realistic case for a brand-new question) walks every candidate run for that
provider via individual `pread`s and costs low seconds at 100k (2.3–2.5 s p50, 3.5–4.8 s p95) — this is the
same `O(candidates)` behavior the pre-existing `test/unit/ledger-reuse-scale.test.ts` already documents and
budgets extra test time for, now paying a real per-call SQLite open cost on top of it. `rebuild` (26.9 s p50 at
100k) is markedly slower than both the spike's own measurement (8.5–9.9 s) and the old JSON index's (3.2 s) on
this run. The db/log ratio came out **1.158 at 10k (over 1.0) and 0.41 at 100k** — inside the schema's "well
under 1.0" design goal only at the larger size, not at 10k, on this run. None of this changes the binding
invariant (deleting or corrupting `index.db` never changes an answer, only speed — proven by the equivalence and
self-heal tests) but it does mean the < 100 ms target and the schema's own db/log ratio goal are reported here
as **not cleanly met at these sizes on this machine**, honestly, rather than picked from a nicer run. The most
likely cause, not fully isolated: `PRAGMA quick_check` (part of every self-heal check, so every fresh open) scans
meaningfully more of the file as the db grows, and this run's per-call numbers scale with db size in a way the
spike's didn't — see "What didn't meet target, and why" below.

## db size vs log size

| n | log bytes | db bytes | db/log ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 15,325,751 | 17,747,968 | 1.158 |
| 100,000 | 153,512,284 | 62,951,424 | 0.410 |

The schema is slim by design (no full JSON copy — `runs.wise` is a small blob, bodies are read back from the
ledger by offset), so the *shape* of the ratio dropping as n grows (fixed per-database overhead — schema, a few
indexes — amortizing over more rows) is expected; that it starts **above 1.0 at 10k** was not. Not chased further
under this task's time budget; flagged as a real number, not smoothed over.

### wise json_extract query (group by $.wise.area)

Opened directly against the built `index.db` (not through `IndexHandle` — no verb wires this up yet; the schema
just makes it possible). Demonstrates the design goal: a dynamic field query without a full-ledger scan.

| n | without index ms | with expression index ms |
|---|---|---|
| 10000 | 8.701 | 0.866 |
| 100000 | 144.859 | 9.777 |

An expression index (`CREATE INDEX ... (json_extract(wise, '$.wise.area'))`) turns a full-table scan into a
sub-10 ms lookup at both sizes — a real, measured win for a capability that costs nothing until it's used.

## Before → JSON index → SQLite, at 100k

"Before" is Task 27's linear baseline (pre-index; `bench-ledger-raw.json` in this repo's history). "JSON index"
is Task 29's original design (ff5f3e8), superseded by this task. "SQLite" is this run. The three benches used
different generators (Task 27/29's default synthetic mix, 1–3 keys/run, vs this task's 10–20 keys/run — the
realism gap `2026-09-26-ledger-lookup-comparison.md` documents), so this is directional, not a byte-identical
apples-to-apples comparison; row-by-row caveats are called out where the shapes genuinely differ.

| op | Before (linear) p50 | JSON index p50 | SQLite p50 | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reuse lookup, **hit** | 1,183.9 ms (`lookupAnswers`, O(provider runs)) | 68.3 ms | 93.2 ms | JSON index's row is also a hit-only sample (its own doc: "only samples keys that already exist"). SQLite is slower here on this run — see "What didn't meet target," below. |
| reuse lookup, **miss** (new question, paid) | same order as hit (no short-circuit) | not separately measured | 2,322.5 ms | The realistic worst case; not measured for the JSON index at 100k with real key volume (its own doc: real keys pushed every load into `REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO`'s rebuild path before this task fixed that). |
| id lookup (`findRun`) | 47.4 ms | 81.7 ms (noisy run, index-parse-dominated) | 130.0 ms | Unchanged code path across Before→JSON index; SQLite replaces the mechanism entirely. |
| rebuild | — | 1,190–3,212 ms (two runs) | 26,873 ms | Slower on SQLite, as the spike itself found (9.9 s) — this run is slower still; see below. |
| `class` (real paid call, checkLedger+reuse+append) | not measured this way | 2.4–8.6 ms (**timed a validation stop, not a real call** — bug (a)) | 799.0 ms | The JSON index's number is not trustworthy (see the task brief); this run's SQLite number is the first real measurement of this exact scenario. |
| db (or index) / log ratio | — (no sidecar) | 0.029–0.031 | 1.158 (10k) / 0.410 (100k) | The JSON sidecar was always far smaller than the log (no schema/index overhead, one JSON blob); SQLite's fixed per-table/per-index overhead makes it comparable to or larger than the log at 10k. |

## What met the < 100 ms target, and what didn't

**Met, on this run:** `reuseHit` and `findRunById` at 10k (29.5 ms / 30.0 ms p50); the `wise` query with its
expression index at both sizes (0.9 ms / 9.8 ms); `catchup1`/`catchup50` at 10k are over target (125–161 ms) but
close.

**Did not meet target, on this run:** everything at 100k except the indexed `wise` query — `reuseHit` (93.2 ms,
just under target on p50 but its own p95 is 169.7 ms), `findRunById` (130.0 ms), `catchup1`/`catchup50`
(608–763 ms), `reuseMiss`/`exactReuseMiss` (2.3–2.5 s), `appendOutcome` (2.96 s), `class` (799.0 ms), `rebuild`
(26.9 s — always expected to be the slow, rare path, but slower here than any prior measurement of it).

This is a materially different picture from `lab/research/2026-09-26-sqlite-spike.md`'s own BLUF ("clears the
< 100 ms target at 100k, on p50, for every operation measured — by a wide margin"). The spike's own generator,
sample counts and exact operations differ from this task's (no `reuseMiss`/`exactReuseMiss` row at all — it only
measured `lookupAnswers` on keys it knew existed), so the two aren't measuring identical things, but the
`rebuild` numbers — the one op both this doc and the spike measure the same way — tell a consistent story:
this run (26.9 s) is slower than the spike's own two runs (8.5 s, 9.9 s), which were themselves slower than the
JSON index's (1.2–3.2 s). Whatever is driving that — machine load at the time (this is a shared box; every prior
2026-09-26 doc in this repo carries the same caveat), or `PRAGMA quick_check`'s cost scaling with `index.db`'s
size on every self-heal check (part of every open, not just rebuild) — is not fully isolated here. What the
equivalence tests (`test/unit/ledger-index.test.ts`, `test/unit/ledger-reuse-scale.test.ts`, both passing against
the real engine in this same container) DO prove: whatever the speed, the answers are identical to the linear
oracle, with the index present, deleted, corrupted, or stale. Binding #1 (only speed changes, never an answer)
holds; binding #2's "< 100 ms" framing does not, cleanly, at 100k, on this run.

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run — out of scope for this task's bench (10k and 100k only, per the brief) and, independently, Task 27's
own finding still applies: `toJsonl`-shaped generation runs into Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH`
(≈512 MiB) somewhere north of ~500,000 records on this build. Extrapolating from the two real points above:
log bytes grow ~10x from 10k→100k (15.3 MB → 153.5 MB), so a 1,000,000-run ledger would be on the order of
**~1.5 GB of log**; `index.db` grew from 17.7 MB (10k) to 63.0 MB (100k) — sub-linearly (the ratio dropped from
1.158 to 0.410 as fixed overhead amortized) — so a rough extrapolation puts a 1M `index.db` somewhere in the
**200–400 MB** range, not a clean 10x of the 100k number; this is a shape a reader should expect, not a number
this doc stands behind as measured. `rebuild`'s own p50 grew from 1,333.9 ms to 26,872.6 ms across the same 10x
step (a ~20x increase) — a 1M rebuild would plausibly land in the **minutes**, not seconds, on a machine under
similar load. None of this is measured; it exists to set expectations before anyone runs it for real.

## Rebuild / maintenance cadence

Unlike the JSON index (which needed `REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO`, a proactive "rebuild once the sidecar gets too big
relative to the log" threshold, because its in-memory maps — `runOffset`, `blocked`, `runIdsNewestFirst` — only
ever grew, never compacted, and a rebuild was the only way to shed that growth), **this design needs no
proactive, size-triggered rebuild at all.** A SQL table's rows grow proportionally with the ledger itself (one
row per run in `runs`, one row per distinct `(who, key)` in `answer_keys` — self-compacting via `INSERT OR
REPLACE`, exactly like the old design's `reuseKey`), and a catch-up only ever touches the bytes actually added
since the last one, so `index.db` never accumulates the kind of dead weight the JSON sidecar did. The measured
cadence is therefore purely reactive, exactly as designed (binding #4): rebuild only on missing, unreadable, a
failed `quick_check`, a schema-version mismatch, a log shorter than `upto`, or a fingerprint mismatch (the
self-heal test suite proves every one of these five triggers a correct rebuild, and a pure-growth case does not).
The one operational number worth carrying forward from this run: if `rebuild` genuinely costs 27 s at 100k
(worth re-measuring on a quieter machine before treating it as load-bearing), an owner restoring from a corrupted
`index.db` on a very large project should expect that order of wait, once, not on every command — every other
command's cost is catch-up (hundreds of ms to low seconds at these sizes on this run), which happens only when
another process's write hasn't been caught up to yet, i.e. essentially never within one command's own single
`withIndex` open.

## What earned its place, and what didn't

**Earned it:** the fingerprint self-heal check (a real bug caught building this task: hashing the in-memory
scan result directly, rather than re-reading the exact same byte range `[fp_start, upto)` the verify-time check
reads, hashed a range that was always one byte short — missing the line's trailing `\n` — so the fingerprint
never matched and every single `withIndex` call rebuilt from scratch, even on an unchanged ledger; fixed by
hashing via one shared `hashLogRange` function on both the write and verify sides, so they can never disagree
about which bytes they're hashing). The in-process memory-fallback cache (Node 20, or any SQLite call throwing):
without it, a static ledger's repeated reads within one process — the exact shape `test/unit/ledger-reuse-scale.test.ts`
exercises — would rescan the whole log on every single call; keyed on the log's own size+mtime, it turns that
into one real scan plus cheap reuse for the rest, and was needed to keep the Node 20 fallback path's own tests
inside a sane time budget.

**Didn't earn a use, but stayed:** the `wise` json_extract query is schema-only — no verb wires it into `view`
or anywhere else yet; the bench measures it because the schema was built to make it possible, not because
anything calls it today. `places`' `kind`/`val` split (where vs. tag) is unused by any bench row beyond
`placeBroad`/`placeNarrow`, which only exercise the `where` side (the generator never emits legacy tags).

**Noted, not fixed:** the < 100 ms miss (`reuseHit`/`findRunById` at 100k, `reuseMiss`/`exactReuseMiss` at both
sizes) and the elevated `rebuild`/db-ratio numbers above. The likely next lever, if a future task revisits this:
profile whether `PRAGMA quick_check`'s cost is genuinely scaling with `index.db`'s size on every open (not just
on catch-up/rebuild) — if so, a cheaper freshness check (e.g. trusting the fingerprint alone once schema/version
match, skipping `quick_check` on the common warm-open path) would be the highest-leverage next step, not
attempted here given this task's scope was the index itself, not a follow-on performance pass.
